implementation_notes: The robust Ruby memo is a Hash plus fetch with a block: the block runs only when the key is absent, so a legitimately cached nil or false is still served from the cache - which the popular ||= guard cannot do - and the assignment inside the block stores the computed value. Ruby's own Hash documentation describes fetch as returning the value for a given key and supplying the default through the block, which is the documented primitive being used. Store the Hash in an instance variable for a per-object memo, or in a constant/singleton for a process-wide one; the classic class-based cache is only justified when the memo needs its own policy (size, TTL, metrics).
pitfalls: Arguments must be usable as Hash keys: the documentation requires hash and eql?, and mutating a key after insertion makes the entry unreachable unless the Hash uses compare_by_identity.
An instance-variable memo lives as long as the object; a class-level or constant memo lives for the process and never releases its keys.
Ruby's GVL makes many memo writes look atomic, but Hash is not thread-safe by contract (JRuby and TruffleRuby run the same code in parallel); shared caches need Concurrent::Map or a mutex.
Forgetting to reset the memo in every mutator produces stale derived values that look like correct cache hits.

variants.name: ||= guard for a nullary memo
variants.implementation_notes: The shortest Ruby memo is the ||= guard on an instance variable: the right-hand side runs only when the variable is nil or false, so a single expensive value is computed once and then returned. It is the whole structure for the nullary case - no Hash, no key derivation - and it is why Ruby needs no memoization library for the common pattern of a derived attribute. Its documented-by-behaviour limit is exactly what makes the Hash#fetch form necessary elsewhere: any falsey result is recomputed on the next call, so it must not be used where nil or false are legitimate answers, and it is not atomic across threads beyond the guarantees the implementation gives.
variants.code_sketch:
def index
  @index ||= build_index      # recomputes whenever the value is nil or false
end

def refresh = @index = nil
pitfalls: Falsey results are never cached: nil and false re-trigger the computation on every call (use Hash#fetch with a block for those).
It cannot key on arguments, so it degenerates as soon as the value depends on a parameter.
Two threads can both evaluate the right-hand side; under MRI the interleaving window is small, on other runtimes it is not.
Concurrent access without a memory barrier can expose a partially initialised object to another thread.

variants.name: Concurrent::Map with compute_if_absent (concurrent-ruby)
variants.implementation_notes: When the memo is shared across threads - or the code runs on JRuby/TruffleRuby where Hash really is parallel - concurrent-ruby's Concurrent::Map supplies the atomic primitive: compute_if_absent stores the block's result only if the key is absent, and the documentation states that the method is atomic, which is what makes one computation per key possible without a hand-written mutex. The library also documents the trap that comes with atomic blocks: the atomic methods taking a block must not use the map itself from inside the block or they deadlock. That makes the recursive memo an explicit non-goal here - insert a placeholder or compute the recursion outside the map, and keep the block short.
variants.code_sketch:
Reports = Concurrent::Map.new

def report(key)
  Reports.compute_if_absent(key) { compose(key) }   # atomic; block must not touch Reports
end

def invalidate = Reports.clear
pitfalls: Atomic methods that take a block must not use the same map inside the block - the documentation says this deadlocks, so recursive memoization cannot run through this path.
Concurrent::Map is not semantically equivalent to Hash (ordering is not guaranteed), so code that relies on insertion order must not be migrated blindly.
It adds a gem dependency; for a single-threaded script the Hash#fetch form is simpler and identical in effect.
It stores what the block returns and still has no eviction: unbounded key sets grow the map for the process lifetime.
